column2: Beren Millidge's dated monthly log of his PhD, dead-ends and completion
column4: {"interview_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "A psychology/philosophy/linguistics graduate with little maths or coding background who set out to complete a UK PhD in predictive coding/active inference despite weak supervision and an undirected start.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Undergrad in psychology, philosophy, linguistics; enjoyed neuroscience and coding aspects but had almost no real coding experience", "phase": 0, "evidence": "My background is that I did my undergrad (2013-2016) in Psychology, philosophy, and linguistics ... I discovered that I really enjoyed the neuroscience and coding aspects of my degree and preferred that to theoretical linguistics. Throughout my undergrad I did not learn to code except blindly copypasting and running other people’s matlab scripts for my undergraduate psychology project.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Pursue an AI/ML path and ultimately a PhD using neuroscience-like ideas (predictive coding/active inference)", "phase": 0, "evidence": "So I decided to apply for a Masters in Artificial Intelligence (and machine learning) at the University of Edinburgh, and got in. ... I have always been interested in the nature of intelligence and thought that I would be able to do well applying what I have learned about the human brain and cognition to artificial systems, which ironically turned out to be fairly close to what I did in my PhD", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "action", "label": "Applied for and entered a Masters in Artificial Intelligence at Edinburgh despite weak maths/coding background", "phase": 1, "evidence": "So I decided to apply for a Masters in Artificial Intelligence (and machine learning) at the University of Edinburgh, and got in. At that point, I had no coding background and no maths experience beyond A-level (high-school) other than a psychology statistics course", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "action", "label": "Self-studied maths and Python before the Masters (textbooks, Strang lectures, tutorials)", "phase": 1, "evidence": "During the summer, I bought myself a calculus and linear algebra textbook and did some reading and some exercises but didn’t get far with it particularly ... I did see Gilbert Strang’s linear algebra youtube lectures recommended widely online, and I think I watched about half of them, although I didn’t do any exercises and only picked up a superficial familiarity with linear algebra. I also went through some introductory python tutorials since I thought that was a good idea and sort of got into coding", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "action", "label": "Chose the most mathematically intense ML courses and skipped the remedial programming class", "phase": 1, "evidence": "There were two compulsory courses for an AI masters, a mathematical course (either Introduction to Applied Machine Learning (IAML) or Machine Learning and Pattern Recognition (MLPR) ... so I chose to do MLPR. I also chose to take the course (Accelerated Natural Language Processing) since it was “accelerated” ... If you didn’t know how to program upon entry you had to take an introductory programming course in Java ... so pretended I already knew how to program even though I had only done like one online free python tutorial in my life.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Severe initial struggle with MLPR maths, proofs, and coding", "phase": 1, "evidence": "MLPR was my first problem. ... I remember staring for a very long time at the same notes being intensely confused. ... The homework sheets were my bane as they usually involved proving various linear algebra identities ... and I had never written a proof in my life nor really understood linear algebra at all.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n7", "type": "action", "label": "Worked through intense ML and programming workload, learning core ML topics and neural networks", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I learned an awful lot very quickly about linear algebra, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, matrices, statistics, learning theory, and bayesian inference.\nMLP was also tough. They had us building ANNs from scratch (in numpy) including CNNs from scratch and implementing backprop by ourselves. This was, let’s say, a challenge to somebody who had no coding experience but somehow I managed to get this figured out relatively quickly.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n8", "type": "milestone", "label": "Completed AI Masters coursework and gained foundational ML competence", "phase": 1, "evidence": "The second term was less intense than the first and was mostly consolidating my machine learning knowledge. ... Finally, for the third term we had to come up with a project proposal for our masters dissertation.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Rejected from four preferred ML dissertation projects; assigned 5th-choice supervisor/topic", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I chose four machine learning ones and was rejected from all of them and ended up with my fifth choice Richard Shillcock who wanted me to study models of autistic savantism using neural networks.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "action", "label": "Explored various ML topics and shifted Masters project toward predictive coding/free energy principle", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Throughout, I largely completely avoided the main purpose of the project and instead meandered through various interesting parts of machine learning, including MCMC algorithms, siamese neural networks, and different normalization methods (batch-norm, layer-norm). At this time I also found predictive coding, and the free energy principle ... Nevertheless, the ideas were sufficiently interesting that I ended up pivoting my masters thesis towards this ending up with a mashup of my original project with predictive coding – ending up proposing an predictive processing model of autism and autistic savantism, supported by neural network experiments.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "milestone", "label": "Masters thesis on predictive processing model of autism received distinction and best dissertation prize", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Somehow, despite all logic, this thesis ended up getting a distinction and indeed winning prize for the best dissertation of the year – which I do not understand at all.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "milestone", "label": "Offered a PhD position by Masters supervisor Richard", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Nevertheless, despite my rather dilettantish work, my supervisor Richard was sufficiently impressed to offer me a PhD position.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Initial failed job search; no interview invitations", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I was initially uncertain as to whether to take it, and briefly tried looking for jobs. After spending about two weeks applying for jobs, talking to recruiters and failing to get to interviews (I was not invited to a single interview – I still don’t know why. I guess I must be really bad at phone screens!)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n14", "type": "action", "label": "Decided to accept the funded PhD position", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I decided to just go for the PhD, which came with a £12000/year tax-free government stipend. Considering that entry level jobs in computer science/AI paid only around £25000 a year in salary in Edinburgh, UK, I decided that this was not actually that great an opportunity cost and went for it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n15", "type": "start_state", "label": "Entered PhD with weak, hands-off supervision and undirected mindset", "phase": 2, "evidence": "mine was unusual in several aspects, especially in having very weak and hands-off supervision for most of the time except for my year in Sussex. Also, I feel like I was much more undirected and unsure about what I wanted to do than most other PhD students", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "goal", "label": "Complete a UK PhD requiring 1–2.5 publishable pieces of work, ideally in strong venues", "phase": 2, "evidence": "UK PhDs are only three to three and a half years long (I got funding from the UK government) and to obtain a PhD the standard is about 1-2.5 publishable pieces of work. ... My understanding of US machine learning PhDs is that they effectively require publication in a top-tier machine learning conference which I have tried (but failed) to achieve in my PhD (I would only succeed at this in my postdoc).", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "n17", "type": "action", "label": "Spent first ~6 months of PhD learning to code for startup ideas, building Android apps, websites, APIs", "phase": 2, "evidence": "At this point I was also reading too much hackernews and enamoured of starting a startup, which I was sure would be fairly easy. I got reasonably far with coding and learnt to code android apps as well as simple websites and APIs, including in PHP and Django python. I also learnt a lot of javascript. This took up much of the first six months of my PhD.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n18", "type": "milestone", "label": "Built an app for startup idea but failed to find investors and shelved project", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I ended up producing an app of my idea but failed to find any investors and the prospect of actually going out and talking to potential customers scared me so much I never did it and eventually shelved the project.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n19", "type": "action", "label": "Started original PhD project on multimodal autoencoder predictive coding; wrote Keras-based paper and posted on psyarxiv", "phase": 2, "evidence": "My original PhD research project which Richard intended me to work on was developing further ideas from my master’s project. The idea was that if we split the input into separate modalities ... and then used an autoencoder ... So I set about trying to do this. ... in a couple of months, by December 2017 had worked up a decent set of experiments and a basic paper on this. I wasn’t very keen on it at all and thought it was pretty rubbish, but wrote it up and put it on psyarxiv.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n20", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Recognised early PhD outputs (papers, side projects) as low-quality and not useful", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I had been at it for almost a year and still had produced nothing particularly useful. ... I wasn’t very keen on it at all and thought it was pretty rubbish ... This paper ended up being so rubbish that I didn’t even put it on psyarxiv", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n21", "type": "event", "label": "Got engaged and married to Mycah; took extended honeymoon and trips, reducing PhD work", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Also at this time (February 2018), I proposed to Mycah and we got engaged. We took a three week working holiday to Prague ... October 2018: I got married to Mycah and took a two week honeymoon which took up most of the month. Minimal PhD work was done.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n22", "type": "obstacle", "label": "After >1 year of PhD, still no publishable work or clear thesis topic; feeling adrift and disillusioned", "phase": 3, "evidence": "June 2018: By this time I was feeling pretty adrift in my PhD. I had been at it for almost a year and still had produced nothing particularly useful. ... November 2018: After the honeymoon was over, I returned to a very disappointing PhD situation. I had been doing a PhD for more than a year and had produced no publishable work and didn’t even know what I was to work on for my main thesis.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n23", "type": "action", "label": "Committed to focusing entirely on predictive coding and free energy principle; deeply studied key papers", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I decided I needed to focus on a single topic, as a lack of focus had been my major problem previously. I decided to focus entirely on predictive coding and the free energy principle, since that was the only thing that had continuously held my interest for more than a year although I had never studied it formally. ... I sat down and exhaustively studied the Buckley tutorial, and the Friston 2003 and 2005 papers in depth and tried to understand everything. It took me about two weeks to understand just those two papers.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n24", "type": "action", "label": "Implemented basic predictive coding networks/DEM and wrote initial implementation report", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I spent the rest of December implementing and experimenting with basic predictive coding networks, including dynamical predictive coding networks and DEM (although I didn’t fully understand it mathematically). ... by the end of January I had written up this “paper”, or really a report (paper and code) which goes through my progress in implementing these models.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n25", "type": "action", "label": "Started daily habit of watching lecture videos to build maths/CS foundations", "phase": 3, "evidence": "Also at this time I decided that I was too far behind in various mathematical and computer science prerequisites and started a habit I maintained throughout 2019 and some of 2020 of spending two hours or more a day watching lecture videos to increase my understanding of key topics.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n26", "type": "action", "label": "Attempted original work combining predictive coding and active inference on cart-pole; wrote and submitted paper to Cognitive Science", "phase": 3, "evidence": "February 2019: I wanted to do something original and decided to combine the predictive coding and active inference models I was working on together to see if I could produce anything useful. I spent most of February working on this on the simple Cart-pole environment ... March 2019: I also focused on getting these cart-pole results out which I did about the middle of March. This resulted in this this paper and code ... I submitted it to the journal cognitive science and eventually, got at least neural responses and revisions instead of a pure rejection.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n27", "type": "action", "label": "Studied deep reinforcement learning and control as inference; tried and failed to replicate David Ha’s world models in Julia", "phase": 3, "evidence": "Towards the end of March I also started getting into deep reinforcement learning, and especially control as inference. ... I also learnt Julia and implemented some simple reinforcement learning models. ... Stupidly, I decided to first try to replicate the David Ha paper entirely in Julia using Flux, which meant I spent more than a month futilely fighting with Flux and attempting to get the model working without success. This was a huge mistake and I never got this working.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n28", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Nearly two years into PhD with no published papers; strong worry about progress", "phase": 3, "evidence": "June 2019: Now almost two years into my PhD and I had no papers. I was getting worried.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n29", "type": "milestone", "label": "Produced and published first decent paper: Deep active inference as variational policy gradients", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I focused completely on this paper as deep active inference and eventually gave up on trying to replicate the David Ha paper and instead just focused on building a super simple actor-critic agent ... This eventually worked and by the end of June I had written up my first decent paper (Deep active inference as variational policy gradients (paper and code). This is the first paper I think was publishable quality and in fact was my first published paper – after TWO YEARS of PhD work.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n30", "type": "event", "label": "Presented deep active inference work at Sussex; met Chris Buckley and Alec Tschantz; invited for research visit", "phase": 4, "evidence": "I had emailed Chris and Manuel about my new paper which I had out and they invited me down to Sussex to talk about it. This ended up being a crucial conversation which would eventually lead to them inviting me down to Brighton for a research visit which would last all of 2020, where I effectively joined their team, and which ultimately made my PhD. I gave the talk in the last week of July. After giving the talk I started chatting to Alec Tschantz another PhD student at Sussex who was working on similar ideas; we agreed to collaborate on extending our deep active inference work after we returned", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n31", "type": "milestone", "label": "Contacted by Giovanni Pezzulo about potential postdoc in Rome", "phase": 4, "evidence": "Other things also started moving. I was contacted by Giovanni Pezzulo who was impressed with my work and wanted to recruit me for a postdoc in Rome, Italy after my PhD.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n32", "type": "event", "label": "Attended Free Energy principle conference; secured 2020 research placement with Chris Buckley", "phase": 4, "evidence": "Crucially, I also attended at the beginning of November a conference in Edinburgh on the Free Energy principle and predictive processing. ... Crucially, I also chatted with Christopher Buckley, who offered a research placement in his lab in 2020, which I accepted. We agreed I would start in early January.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n33", "type": "event", "label": "Moved from Edinburgh to Brighton to start Sussex research fellowship; began working closely with Alec and Chris", "phase": 5, "evidence": "January 2020: On the 2nd of January 2020, Mycah and I loaded everything into a van and drove down from Edinburgh to Brighton to take up the research fellowship at the university of Sussex. I started officially on Jan 4th. For the first month there, Alec and I worked very closely on our ideas of merging active inference with deep reinforcement learning.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n34", "type": "milestone", "label": "Produced deep RL/active inference paper and influential expected free energy paper with Sussex mentorship", "phase": 5, "evidence": "Feburary 2020: I spent a lot of time honing our model-based reinforcement learning paper (Reinforcement learning through active inference) and submitting that to the workshop. Also, I focused heavily on writing up my thoughts on the expected free energy, resulting in this paper, which is my second paper to be published in a journal, and one which I am very proud of. I think these two papers of early 2020 represent me finally breaking through the research barrier and making real, if small, contributions to the state of the art in various fields.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n35", "type": "action", "label": "Developed hybrid predictive coding with feedforward sweep and biologically plausible backprop work", "phase": 5, "evidence": "March 2020: Chris and Alec had ideas about adding a ‘feedforward sweep’ to predictive coding models using amortized inference, like variational autoencoders. ... I managed to make this mathematically precise and coded up the first implementation. ... The predictive coding algorithm which would eventually became this paper (and code), and implemented the first versions of these relaxations to show that they worked. By the beginning of April I had written up a first draft of the relaxed predictive coding paper to show them.\n... May 2020: I became heavily interested in biologically plausible backprop ... working on my proof and paper showing that predictive coding approximates backprop on arbitrary computation graphs. ... This resulted in this paper and code which got rejected from Neurips, although it got shared widely on twitter and has become my most popular paper.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n36", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Funding end approaching; few savings; anxiety about post-PhD employment", "phase": 6, "evidence": "I also started to get seriously worried about finding a job to do after my PhD. My PhD funding was meant to run out in September (3 years from September 2017) but was extended by the UK government for another 6 months due to Covid. Due to only earning £12000 / year I had only a few months’ savings and could not live for a long time without any additional money.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n37", "type": "action", "label": "Applied simultaneously to postdoc with Rafal Bogacz and to Entrepreneur First; considered second startup", "phase": 6, "evidence": "I also thought about applying for postdocs and here I found Rafal Bogacz’ postdoc in Oxford. He had reached out to Chris and me a few months back about the predictive coding paper and I saw that he had a postdoc available on his website, so I restarted the conversation and applied.\nAnother thing I was considering doing was another startup. ... I also applied to Entrepreneur First (EF) and got through to their first stage and would ultimately get an offer which I rejected to instead do the postdoc.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n38", "type": "milestone", "label": "Received offers from both Entrepreneur First and Rafal’s postdoc; accepted the postdoc", "phase": 6, "evidence": "October 2020: ... I also went through interviews for Rafal’s postdoc and EF and got acceptances for both and spent a lot of time agonizing about what I should actually do. ... I ultimately decided to accept the postdoc with Rafal instead of going for a startup at EF.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n39", "type": "outcome", "label": "Completed a PhD with multiple predictive coding/active inference contributions and secured a postdoc with Rafal Bogacz", "phase": 7, "evidence": "As my PhD comes to an end, it is time to reflect back on three and a half years of work, struggle, failure, and some minor successes eventually culminating in the dreaded PhD thesis. ... During the summer, I bought myself a calculus and linear algebra textbook and did some reading and some exercises\"; \"I also went through some introductory python tutorials\"", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r5", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not neglect doing exercises and proofs when learning mathematics; avoid superficial familiarity", "evidence": "\"I think I watched about half of them, although I didn’t do any exercises and only picked up a superficial familiarity with linear algebra.\"; \"The homework sheets were my bane… and I had never written a proof in my life nor really understood linear algebra at all.\"", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r6", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use difficult homework and proofs as tools to deeply learn linear algebra, statistics, and Bayesian inference", "evidence": "\"The homework sheets were my bane… and I had never written a proof in my life nor really understood linear algebra at all. In retrospect this was a pretty bad idea which would have sucked up a lot of time for relatively little gain.\"", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r23", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Recognize and drop lines of work that are not enjoyable or motivating, even if they are technically feasible", "evidence": "\"I rapidly discovered that doing statistical analyses of eye tracking experiments is not particularly what I enjoyed doing and I found it hard to have a lot of motivation for the questions we were investigating.\"; \"I was rapidly disillusioned with this and basically stopped.\"", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r24", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Monitor your funding timeline and begin planning jobs or postdoc applications well before your PhD stipend ends", "evidence": "\"My PhD funding was meant to run out in September (3 years from September 2017) but was extended by the UK government for another 6 months due to Covid.\"; \"I also thought about applying for postdocs and here I found Rafal Bogacz’ postdoc in Oxford.\"", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r25", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Evaluate startup programs, investment terms, and your own goals critically before choosing between academia and entrepreneurship", "evidence": "\"I also applied to Entrepreneur First (EF) and got through to their first stage and would ultimately get an offer which I rejected to instead do the postdoc.\"; \"This was for a couple of reasons. It makes it easy to look me up and provides information about me in a condensed manner.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r24", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use easy website tooling such as GitHub Pages or Jekyll to build a one-page site", "evidence": "One can easily use GitHub Pages or Jekyll to create a one-page website.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r25", "primitive": "Op", "label": "When writing a narrative SOP, tell your story chronologically, highlight turning points, community and research experiences, future goals, and school fit", "evidence": "My first trial’s SOP is a beautifully written thing. It told my story chronologically, and a reviewer could see all the turning points. I started with my interest in CS and AI, my BSc at FUNAAB, and the research project I did as an undergraduate. Then I wrote about how ML Collective has been helpful for my research journey and a research assistantship role that I picked up with a German DFKI researcher. Then finally, my knowledge-sharing efforts via community, my future goals, and why this school is my choice.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r26", "primitive": "Op", "label": "For ultra-competitive AI PhD programs, consider a SOP that is mainly a research statement emphasizing concrete research directions", "evidence": "In my second attempt, it was more of a research statement than a personal statement.\nBut AI is an ultra-competitive field and easily has more than 4x the number of graduate school candidates in any other area, and everybody is terribly smart. It makes sense to cut out the fillers and self-serenades and strip to the bones quickly to stand out. How? By talking about the main goal of a PhD: research! ALL the best SOPs I have seen at the most competitive AI PhD programs do this.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r27", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Organize your research-focused SOP by breaking your main interest into sub-areas and dedicating a paragraph to each", "evidence": "I split my research interest, ML efficiency, into three categories: data efficiency, efficiency in algorithms & methods, and efficiency in systems & applications, and dedicated a paragraph to each.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r28", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Include a concise paragraph on your professional growth and compress broader personal narrative into a small section", "evidence": "Aside from the introduction and the closing paragraphs, the only other paragraph was titled “Growing professionally,” and I compressed what could have formed another personal statement on its own into a single paragraph.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r29", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Mention specific professors you want to work with rather than extended generic school praise", "evidence": "I barely talked about why I wanted to attend the school, except to mention the list of professors I wanted to work with.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r30", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Ensure that even a research-heavy SOP remains deeply personalized and that all stated research areas are clearly connected", "evidence": "Pro-tip: While SOP is solely focused on the research you want to do, it has to be deeply personalized. And all the mentioned research areas must connect!", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r31", "primitive": "Branch", "label": "Do you already have a clear, specific research interest?", "evidence": "But if an applicant doesn’t have a clear research interest yet, writing the second way could prove a disaster. It automatically limits the kind of professors one could work with, and you may have schools where nobody works at that intersection.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r32", "primitive": "Op", "label": "If you lack a clear research interest, avoid a tightly focused research-only SOP and use a broader, story-driven style", "evidence": "But if an applicant doesn’t have a clear research interest yet, writing the second way could prove a disaster.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r33", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Mitigate the risk of overly narrow interests by searching for schools and professors across your broader area of interest", "evidence": "The way I searched for schools and professors mitigates that potential problem.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r34", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Be aware that higher-ranked schools often have faculty with narrower interests and less openness to topics outside their field", "evidence": "Also, I noticed that the faculty tended to be narrower and less interested in topics outside their field as the school's ranking rose.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r35", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Secure recommendation letters primarily from professors and research scientists, then lecturers, employers, or postdocs", "evidence": "As a general rule of thumb, letters from professors and research scientists count the most. After that, rank letters from lecturers, employers, or postdocs.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r36", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Choose recommenders who know your research capacity well and can write enthusiastically about it", "evidence": "Naturally, all recommenders are familiar with one’s research capacity and can write enthusiastically about it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r37", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Prefer recommenders who are known or respected within your subfield, as committees may recognize their names", "evidence": "A letter counts a lot more if the admissions committee knows the recommender. Usually, the top researchers in the same subfield know each other.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r38", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Leverage relationships with your department’s more senior faculty when they know your work and activities well", "evidence": "On the second attempt, I used my HoD, the highest-ranking professor in my department. I asked him only because I had helped with some code implementation in one of his large-scale, multi-departmental projects and because he is very familiar with my extracurricular activities due to my collaborations with the department in my capacity as the community lead for the Google Developer Students Club.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r39", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Seek application fee waivers through schools that offer free PhD applications, diversity waivers, or affiliation-based waivers", "evidence": "Some schools, like Rice, offer free PhD applications. Some schools usually have sessions where they publicize fee waivers. I am immensely thankful for my Black in AI affiliation. Schools like UW, CMU, and MIT offer waivers if you can prove your affiliation with BAI. A few, like Stanford, have a diversity/URM waiver where you have to write about how you are disadvantaged.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r40", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Plan applications around typical US CS PhD deadlines in December through February and start early enough to avoid a rush", "evidence": "Usually, most US schools have application submission deadlines around December 15. Some are as early as December 1st or 8th, and some are as late as January or February.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r41", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Reuse SOP content where possible to speed up repeated application form filling", "evidence": "Filling out the applications repeatedly is always a chore. Since I did not have to change a lot in my SOP, I moved fast this time and submitted all my applications around December 8th.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r42", "primitive": "Op", "label": "During interviews, be very confident in your research work and able to defend every point in your SOP and CV", "evidence": "The bottom line is to be very confident about your research work and be able to defend every single point in your SOP and CV.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r43", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not attempt to bluff or ‘bullshit’ through technical interview questions with experts in your field", "evidence": "The interviewer is most likely an expert in your field of interest or a similar field, so you cannot bullshit your way through (I tried it in one of my first-time attempts, and it didn’t work).", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r44", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Identify and fill gaps in your core knowledge before interviews to avoid appearing confused or overwhelmed", "evidence": "In hindsight, I wasn’t convincing enough in my interviews for my first trial. There were too many gaps in my knowledge of machine learning and deep learning.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r45", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Avoid agreeing too readily with interviewers’ conjectures when your understanding is weak", "evidence": "I agreed too readily with most conjectures from my interviewers since I knew little (CU Boulder and Northeastern).", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r46", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Handle trap questions about competing offers by deflecting rather than answering too bluntly", "evidence": "And in one of the calls, I got asked a trap question (“What school will give you an offer that’d make you reject our offer?”) and was too honest. The wiser me deflected a similar question in my second trial.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r47", "primitive": "Op", "label": "When choosing between offers, examine funding type: TA, RA tied to advisor’s grant, or independent research fellowship", "evidence": "The first is the kind of funding. Usually, funding comes in the form of graduate (teaching or research) assistantships or a research fellowship. A teaching assistantship requires you to teach alongside your research, while a research assistantship is tied to your advisor’s funding, so you’d have to work within the field of your advisor’s grant. Either requires 20 hours of work per week. A research fellowship is usually not tied to any obligations and is mainly funded by external bodies like the NSF.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r48", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Assess potential advisors’ values, mentoring and research style, communication preferences, and balance between wellbeing and research progress", "evidence": "It is also imperative to understand an advisor’s values, mentoring or research style, and what constitutes a good fit for you. Hands-on vs. hands-off? Confrontational or indirect communication style? Discretion vs. in-group cohesion? Well-being vs. research progress, et cetera.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r49", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Talk to current students of potential advisors and learn about the program and living conditions before accepting an offer", "evidence": "School visitation or speaking with your potential advisor’s students is also necessary. You’d want to understand what people who interact with your advisor think about them. It’s also not trivial to know more about the program and the living conditions in the school’s city. I had calls with three CMU students around this.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r50", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Provide unofficial transcripts with applications and arrange for official transcripts to be sent once admitted, following each school’s rules", "evidence": "Usually, it is required to submit one’s (unofficial) transcripts during the application process, and once a school accepts one, it is required for the student’s former institution to send the full, official transcripts to the new institution.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r51", "primitive": "Op", "label": "As an undergraduate applicant, submit all available semesters and send full official transcripts before starting the program", "evidence": "It’s not important to submit your full transcripts if you are an undergrad. You can submit everything else aside from your last two semesters in undergrad. Of course, the official, full transcripts have to be received before you resume the program.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r52", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Initiate visa processes (DS-160, SEVIS, MRV fee, interview scheduling) soon after receiving the i-20, ideally before June or July", "evidence": "Usually, the school issues an i-20 sometime in April or May, and then visa applications can commence. There will be a DS-160 form, and you'll have to pay for SEVIS. Then you pay the MRV fee to schedule an F-1 visa interview date. Naturally, lots of people panic about this, but there is actually no reason to do that, especially if you do all this before June or July.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r53", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Read a few visa interview transcripts, especially for funded students, to understand common questions", "evidence": "I think it helps to read a few interview transcripts beforehand to understand the kind of questions to expect, but you'll most likely feel understimulated and unstretched when you interview. I read a couple of transcripts via Nairaland and a WhatsApp group, and usually, it is the non-funded and partially-funded students that struggle during the visa interviews.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r54", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not over-invest in extensive mock visa interviews or anxiety if you are fully funded", "evidence": "For the interview preparation, there is usually lots of pressure to do lots of mock interviews and get prayerful, but you honestly don’t need to do any of that if you are going for a fully funded graduate program.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r55", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Attend your visa interview comfortably dressed and without needing to arrive excessively early", "evidence": "For the interview itself, you don’t have to be there super early. And you don’t have to dress uncomfortably formally. Wearing suits in very humid weather or heels when you'd standing and queueing for a long stretch of time might not be super comfortable. The consular officer probably doesn’t care. I wore jeans and a round-neck T-shirt, and I was fine.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r56", "primitive": "Op", "label": "After visa approval, arrange accommodation and flights, using school-provided guides and advice from current students", "evidence": "After this, all that should be left are accommodations and booking flights. The school usually provides guides on the former. {"interview_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "A new MSc student at UBC in computer science, initially without an advisor and vaguely interested in machine learning, navigating research, papers, and future career decisions.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Arrives at UBC for MSc, funded research-based program, no advisor, broadly interested in ML", "phase": 0, "evidence": "Fresh off of my undergraduate degree and two months of backpacking across Europe and Asia, I came to Vancouver energized, optimistic and completely clueless. In hopes of finding a research advisor, I told every student/professor that I met that I was “broadly interested in machine learning”

- Some master’s students start the program without a committed research advisor and are expected to find one after their first year. I was one of these cases.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Find a research advisor and research direction", "phase": 0, "evidence": "In hopes of finding a research advisor, I told every student/professor that I met that I was “broadly interested in machine learning”", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "obstacle", "label": "ML lab unlikely to take unknown, unfunded student", "phase": 1, "evidence": "On the first day of my orientation, one of the PhD students in the ML lab tells me that the chance of an unknown, unfunded student joining their lab is virtually zero.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "action", "label": "Cold-email ML-adjacent professors seeking meetings", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I found any ML-adjacent professor I could and sent them cold emails asking for meetings.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Cold emails to ML-adjacent professors ignored or forgotten", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Every single one of these emails was ignored or forgotten.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "action", "label": "Focus on three graduate courses including Ivan's distributed systems course", "phase": 1, "evidence": "The rest of my mental energy and time this semester was spent completely on three graduate courses. In one of these courses, Ivan’s distributed systems course, the entire course consisted of reading, reviewing, and discussing papers everyday in class;", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n7", "type": "event", "label": "Ivan emails inviting consideration of working with him as advisor", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Once I land back in Toronto to visit my family over the winter holidays, Ivan sends me an email, asking if I would consider working with him as his student.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n8", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Feels scared due to knowing very little about distributed systems", "phase": 1, "evidence": "The prospect sounds exciting but I know very little about distributed systems which scares me.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "action", "label": "Meets with Ivan and agrees to become his student", "phase": 2, "evidence": "After spending the winter holidays considering my one-and-only option, I meet with Ivan in the first week of January and agree to be his student.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "milestone", "label": "Establishes regular paper reading and discussions to build research taste", "phase": 2, "evidence": "every week I read a few papers, took notes on them, and discussed my thoughts with Ivan. Our lab also hosted a weekly reading group that featured lively discussion about recent papers published in top conferences.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "milestone", "label": "Becomes socially comfortable and builds community at UBC", "phase": 2, "evidence": "this was the term in which I really started to get more comfortable at UBC socially. In addition to forming a community with my research labmates, I really began to connect with the wider CS department as a whole.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "event", "label": "Google publishes federated learning blog post, becomes basis of research", "phase": 3, "evidence": "In April of 2017, Google published a blog post introducing federated learning: the topic that would end up being the basis of my research for the next 2 years.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "action", "label": "Starts first full-time research term, initial project on peer-to-peer federated learning with privacy and security", "phase": 3, "evidence": "This was the first term in which I did research full-time, with no other course or TA obligations. I’ve never written a serious, non-course-project paper before, so the thought of making new research claims to completely anonymous reviewers is absolutely terrifying. For about four weeks straight, I work frantic and disorganized late nights leading up to the submission deadline, which is more intense and stressful than anything I have ever done. At the end of a 36-hour non-stop work session, we submit with 30 seconds remaining.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "action", "label": "Moves into basement apartment in Kitsilano with cohort friends despite poor conditions", "phase": 4, "evidence": "I move in with some of my UBC cohort friends to a basement apartment in Kitsilano. I’ll be completely honest here: my Master’s thesis was just my latest TorMentor submission with formatting adjustments.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n25", "type": "milestone", "label": "Master's thesis easily approved with minor formatting fixes", "phase": 7, "evidence": "my master’s thesis was easily approved with minor formatting fixes, and I highly doubt that anybody has read it in full since.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n26", "type": "goal", "label": "Commit to a career in CS research rather than software engineering job", "phase": 7, "evidence": "By this point, I knew that a software engineering job was not of interest to me and I was committed to a career in CS research, so a PhD was the natural next choice.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n27", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Wants to move away from distributed systems to ML security and privacy research", "phase": 7, "evidence": "Despite being very productive working with Ivan for two years, I was looking to move away from distributed systems research and wanted to branch more into machine learning security and privacy research.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n28", "type": "event", "label": "Ivan offers PhD spot at UBC but encourages applying elsewhere", "phase": 7, "evidence": "Ivan offered that I could stay on as his PhD student at UBC, but strongly encouraged me to at least apply elsewhere.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n29", "type": "action", "label": "Collaborates with Ivan on shortlist and PhD applications; applies to 8 programs", "phase": 7, "evidence": "Most PhD programs accept applications in December, so there was plenty of time for Ivan and I to collaborate on a shortlist of potential advisors and my application. One should ideally start writing rough drafts at least by the beginning of September (for December deadlines).", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r23", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Carefully read each school’s SoP/essay prompt and tailor your essay to address the specific requested questions", "evidence": "Read the prompt for the essay. Every school (in some cases even departments) have different prompts asking you to answer different questions in the essay.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r24", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use the SoP to explain your motivation, objectives, fit with the program, and any weaknesses (e.g., low GPA or gap year) with genuine reasons", "evidence": "You have to tell them how you would benefit from their program and how you can contribute to their department through research. This is the place where you explain the chinks in your armour like a low GPA, or a gap year. Also, they should be genuine reasons and you should not get obsessed on explaining them in great detail and spend half a page on it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r25", "primitive": "Op", "label": "If changing fields or departments from your bachelor’s degree, clearly explain the switch and how your projects built relevant skills", "evidence": "If you are applying to a department other than the department you got your bachelors degree from, it is important to explain why you are switching fields and why it would be a good match. You should mention how each project you have worked on has helped you acquire particular skills which could help their department in research.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r26", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Write initial SoP drafts in a modular way so common content can be reused across universities, then personalize each SoP", "evidence": "Another important thing to remember while writing the SoP is that you should write your first few drafts in such a way that you can transfer its contents to the SoPs for all the universities... But while doing this it is also quite necessary to personalise each SoP for particular universities.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r27", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Avoid reading sample SoPs before drafting your own first version to preserve uniqueness", "evidence": "Also, I would recommend at not looking at sample SoPs on the internet before writing your first draft as it would take away the uniqueness of your SoP as your SoP would get biased towards the samples you have seen before.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r28", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Get your SoP reviewed by people from varying backgrounds to ensure clarity for both technical and non-technical readers", "evidence": "I feel that it is important to get the essay reviewed by people from varying backgrounds as your SoP might get quite technical and you do not know who is going to read your SoP in the admissions committee... This is where your diverse set of “SoP reviewers” will help.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r29", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Ask potential recommenders early (as early as August) if they are willing to provide strong letters of recommendation", "evidence": "Ask your academic advisors, internship guides or professors if they are willing to give strong letters of recommendations.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r30", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Prioritize recommenders who know your research capabilities and have worked closely with you or taught you multiple courses", "evidence": "Generally, the adcom expects LoRs from people with whom you have worked quite closely and ideally for a considerable duration. Also, it is quite important to ask your (possible) recommenders whether they would be willing to give LoRs quite early (as early as August). It is also okay to take an LoR from a professor who has taught you more than one course or with whom you have had frequent interactions. It is quite important that they should be able to write about your research capabilities.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r31", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Explicitly ask recommenders whether they can provide a strong recommendation rather than a neutral one", "evidence": "While asking it is important to make sure that you ask your recommender whether he/she will be able to give a strong recommendation. The word “strong” is quite important as some might agree to give recommendation letters just on the basis of knowing you through your grades and not being able to comment on your research capabilities.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r32", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Find out any limits recommenders have on the number of letters and plan your university list and recommender allocation accordingly", "evidence": "Also, some professors have a lot of students asking for recommendation letters and thus will put a cap on the number of recommendation letters he/she will give you... So get to know if there are any restrictions from your recommender as you choose your universities. You could also ask 4 people to give you recommendation letters if there is a cap limit set by one of your recommenders and shuffle them into different universities.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r33", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Provide recommenders with a package including resume, final SoP, transcripts, and relevant papers or technical reports", "evidence": "Once I was ready to send the requests for LoRs through the application portal, I prepared a package for my recommenders which included the following things:
- My updated resume
- My final SoP draft
- Transcripts
- A copy of the paper/technical report of the project on which I worked with him
- This checklist so that they know which profs and universities I am applying to", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r34", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Ask recommenders if they need any additional documents beyond the standard package", "evidence": "You should also ask your recommenders if they require any document other than the ones mentioned above. Generally, they ask you the things they want when you request them for the LoRs.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r35", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Thank recommenders after letters are submitted, for example with a small gift or gesture of appreciation", "evidence": "Once the letters were submitted by my recommenders, I gave each of them a small gift as a token of appreciation for taking out their time to go through the package and writing the letter and submitting them at all the different portals.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r36", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Email professors when applying for PhD programs, preferably before submissions, to ask if they are taking new students and possibly arrange interviews", "evidence": "For PhD applications, it is quite important to mail professors either before or after the application submissions as some professors prefer to take interviews before admitting the student. Preferably it should be done before the submissions so that you can ask them if they will be taking new students.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r37", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Be patient with professor email responses; expect replies during winter holidays and possible Skype chats", "evidence": "Remember, most of the professors are quite busy and my not reply to your mails as quickly as you would expect. It happened with me too, but most of them will reply back during the winter holidays and some may even have a chat with you over Skype to get to know more about your background.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r38", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Prepare to answer common research-oriented questions if professors interview you", "evidence": "I am listing down some of the questions the professors asked me:
- What areas of research interest you?
- Please list the different research experiences you have had.
- What was innovative about your research?
- What was the biggest challenge you encountered in your research, and how did you deal with it?
- If you were starting your project again today, what would you do differently?
- What do you want to work on in my lab?
- What interests you about my research?
- What techniques have you learned that you could use in my lab?", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r39", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Carefully fill out the online application form, uploading required documents and sending LoR requests", "evidence": "Most of the universities have a long form to be filled up on a portal. You upload your resume, SoP, etc. on this portal. You also send LoR requests to your recommenders through this portal. All your details have to be filled in here. So you don’t want to make a mistake here.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r40", "primitive": "Op", "label": "For international students, ensure your name in applications matches your passport", "evidence": "For international students, it is important to fill in your name as it is in your passport.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r41", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use a checklist to track each application’s components and status", "evidence": "I used this checklist for tracking all my applications.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r42", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Thoroughly recheck the entire application before submitting", "evidence": "Just before submitting, I was rechecking the whole application again and again as if my life depended on it.", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r43", "primitive": "Repeat", "label": "Wait for admissions decisions after submitting applications", "evidence": "- Wait!", "certainty": "stated", "stop_condition": "until all admissions decisions are released (generally by 15th April)"}, {"id": "r44", "primitive": "Op", "label": "During the waiting period, pursue hobbies or other activities to de-stress and divert attention from results", "evidence": "I would recommend every one to take these holidays to de-stress yourself and get your attention away from the impending results.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r45", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Recognize that rejections are inevitable and focus on needing only one admit among your applications", "evidence": "It is highly improbable that you will get in all the universities you apply to, so rejections are inevitable. column6: {"source_id": "unknown", "goal": "Break into and do well in a top US Economics PhD program", "domain": "education / academic career (economics PhD)", "nodes": [{"id": "r1", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Recognize that strong recommendation letters are central to top economics PhD admission", "evidence": "To get a top US econ phd, e.g. top 20, you’ll need ‘strong letters’, i.e. strong recommender + strong recommendation.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r2", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Aim to work full-time as a research assistant at a top economics institution to obtain strong letters", "evidence": "The best way to get it is to work as a research assistant for a full year or two at a top institute, e.g. Harvard/MIT/NBER, etc.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r3", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Understand why letters based only on coursework and grades are weaker signals of research potential", "evidence": "Of course you can get letters by taking classes and acing them, but being good at classes is very different from being good at research.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r4", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Recognize that part-time RA experience at your home institution may be insufficient compared to full‑time RA at top places", "evidence": "Why is working as a part-time RA during my undergrad years for a prof. at my undergrad institute not enough?... there are people who has straight As from undergrad, and did a master, and worked as RAs full-time, who has strong letters from their RA bosses who are well plugged into top econ academia. Why would the admissions committee choose you who is a fresh undergrad over them", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r5", "primitive": "Branch", "label": "Do you have an exceptional math signal or embedded elite status in the system?", "evidence": "In other words, you either need an extremely strong and not-noisy signal about your math ability, like the IMO gold medal, or, someone in the system to vouch for you.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r6", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Leverage exceptional math achievements as an alternative path to admission", "evidence": "If you are a IMO gold medalist, you can ignore the above, because your extreme math ability is enough to convince the admission committee", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r7", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use top European or US research‑oriented master programs as alternative pipelines into top US econ PhD if you can rank at the top", "evidence": "Some top European masters program consistently place their top students into top US econ grad schools, e.g. LSE, PSE, TSE, etc. There are some in the US too: Duke has a research-oriented master program in econ. But you basically need to be top 1 or 2 in those to directly place into, say, Harvard/MIT", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r8", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Exploit advantages as a well‑connected Harvard/MIT undergrad with RA and advanced coursework", "evidence": "If you’re a Harvard/MIT undergrad who has started working as a research assistant part-time for the faculty since, say, your sophomore year, and you did well, and took grad classes and Real Analysis, and got As, you can also ignore the above", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r9", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Assess whether potential recommenders are \"in the system\" by checking their prior placement records", "evidence": "How to check if they are ‘in the system’? Check their past placement record. For example, HKUST consistently place their undergrads into BU and Rutgers’ econ phd program, because there’s an already-established relationship.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r10", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Ask faculty explicitly where they think they can realistically place you to infer strength of their letter", "evidence": "And just ask: ‘Do you think I should apply to programs outside of the top 20?’ And that should be a natural starter of an honest conversation on where they think they can realistically place you into, which shows you how strong they are planning to write the letter.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r11", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Prioritize recommenders who understand and use the implicit language and norms of economics rec letters", "evidence": "There’s a certain way to write letters, which ‘everyone in the circle’ knows, and if the letter isn’t written that way, sometimes it’s simply tossed away.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r12", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Target RA positions through official department job posting channels", "evidence": "His answer was surprisingly simple: just go on Harvard’s econ department’s website, and there’s a channel where faculty posts RA job postings.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r13", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Apply for RA roles that match any special skills you have, such as language abilities", "evidence": "What’s more, there’s sometimes work that only me as a foreign student can do — I went on Harvard econ’s website, and found that there is an RA posting particularly looking for Chinese speakers", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r14", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Perform even \"dumb\" or tedious RA tasks with high diligence and structure", "evidence": "If you haven’t realized yet, part-time RAship for undergrads are usually ‘dumb work’... Simple task, right? But to me that’s the only wood board I had in this giant ocean... I have to do it well.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r15", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Systematize and document data work carefully to demonstrate competence", "evidence": "Created an excel where each tab was a different dataset, with a cover page describing the relationship and back-info of each dataset... Under each tab, I had the year/time period the data was collected, what’s a unit of observation, and of course, translation of each variable, and a more detailed description of what the variables meant, and their relationship.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r16", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Capitalize on opportunities to extend RA roles into full‑time and leadership positions", "evidence": "One day, she called me into her office... she asked if I wanted to work for her full-time for the summer... The summer job was more demanding — instead of working alone, I now have to manage a team", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "r17", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Allow your main RA supervisor to guide the strategic shaping of your profile and coursework", "evidence": "You can see that the course taking was very much ‘calculated’, and was communicated between me and MA — that’s the best scenario. Your main letter writer, i.e. RA boss, has the responsibility to ‘sell’, i.e. distribute you. As a result, it’ll be best if they also have discretion over how you shape your profile.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r18", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use undergrad econometrics and graduate econometrics early to build practical research skills", "evidence": "Undergrad econometrics was a ‘bare minimum’... The point is, having A in undergrad Real Analysis is so common nowadays that not having it is a minus.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r20", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use a senior thesis or independent research to give recommenders evidence of research potential", "evidence": "The Senior Thesis Seminar was such that I can work on a piece of independent research under MA’s supervision, so that in her letter she can credibly talk about my research potential.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r21", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Take second‑year field courses largely to generate additional letters and field identity rather than for signal value", "evidence": "The 2nd year grad level Development Economics was such that I can get other rec letters from faculty at Harvard/MIT, i.e. in the circle... 2nd year classes... sometimes everyone gets an A, and as a result there isn’t as much signal value as 1st year classes.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r22", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Avoid first‑year graduate theory courses with high downside risk unless strategically justified", "evidence": "For example, the reason why I did not take any 1st year grad class at Harvard was that, *if* I get, say, a C, then it will be very hard for her to sell me. {"source_id": "unknown", "goal": "Decide on and apply to a PhD program in a way that aligns with your goals, needs, and well-being", "domain": "graduate education / PhD applications and selection", "nodes": [{"id": "r1", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Recognize that there are multiple valid ways to write a PhD SOP and tailor yours to your personality, goals, discipline, and audience", "evidence": "I can’t say this is the only way to write an SOP—consider it just one example of how someone else has approached it. column2: Ben Harrap's PhD: from master's and RA work to thesis submission, alongside a part-time job
column4: {"source_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "A biostatistics graduate working in academic roles who decided to pursue a PhD while maintaining similar income and developed passion and skills during the PhD.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Finished master's in biostatistics and working academic roles", "phase": 0, "evidence": "Back in 2018 I finished my master’s degree in biostatistics and proceeded to work in various roles applying my statistics and data skills. These were predominantly academic positions", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "milestone", "label": "Transition from casual retail to full-time Level A wage", "phase": 0, "evidence": "Going from working a minimum-wage casual retail job to earning a full-time Level A wage felt good by comparison.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "goal", "label": "Long-standing desire to do a PhD", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I’d wanted to do a PhD for a long time", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Concern about being a broke PhD student", "phase": 0, "evidence": "The prospect of being a broke PhD student was not appealing.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "event", "label": "Conversation with friend about working while doing a PhD", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I found out after I chatted to a friend of mine who suggested working a couple of days in addition to doing a PhD.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "action", "label": "Ran the numbers on scholarship plus part-time work income", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I ran the numbers and he was right, if I was able to secure a PhD scholarship (~$30,000 a year tax-free at the time) and work two days a week, my net income was almost the same as my current full-time income as a research assistant.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n7", "type": "action", "label": "Decided to do a PhD treating it like a job", "phase": 1, "evidence": "With this in mind, I figured I may as well do a PhD. Graduate researchers are a source of cheap labour and the work would be similar to what I was currently doing.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n8", "type": "event", "label": "Realised PhD work had much more independence than research assistant role", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Well it turns out the work wasn’t the same as being a research assistant (there is a LOT more independence), but the pay was at least the same.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "start_state", "label": "No passion for a particular area, just enjoyed coding", "phase": 2, "evidence": "At the time however, I wasn’t passionate about any area in particular. I just really enjoyed coding and was agnostic to the context that I was doing it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "action", "label": "Searched advertised projects suited to skills", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Since I didn’t know what I wanted to do, I looked for projects being advertised that were suited to my skills in an area that I thought was interesting.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "milestone", "label": "Found quantitative PhD project on Aboriginal children in out-of-home care", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I happened across an advert on the Statistical Society of Australia’s job forum. I saw an advert for a quantitative PhD student to do research into the health outcomes of Aboriginal children in out-of-home care using linked administrative data.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "milestone", "label": "Developed passion for PhD topic over time", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I was certainly in the latter category initially, however my passion for my topic developed over the course of my PhD.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "action", "label": "Worked 9–5, five days a week; three on PhD, two in job", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I worked 9 to 5, five days a week - three being on my PhD and two being in my job.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n14", "type": "event", "label": "COVID and remote working increased flexibility", "phase": 3, "evidence": "The advent of covid and remote working was a boon, because it meant I could be a lot more flexible with my time.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n15", "type": "action", "label": "Varied weekly allocation between PhD and job as needed", "phase": 3, "evidence": "Some weeks I might work 5 days on my PhD and make up work days at a later date - as long as the work got done nobody minded.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "action", "label": "Chose to learn R and RMarkdown instead of Stata and Word", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I could have stuck with Stata and written my thesis in MS Word, but I wanted to learn R so I committed to doing as much as possible in R and RMarkdown.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n17", "type": "action", "label": "Implemented unfamiliar statistical methods where possible", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I could have used statistical methods I had used before, but where possible I made sure to implement methods I hadn’t.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n18", "type": "obstacle", "label": "First research article took two years from initial meeting to publication", "phase": 4, "evidence": "In reality, two years passed between the first meeting to discuss the aims of the article and when it was finally published.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n19", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Underestimated timelines for second article; took nine months", "phase": 4, "evidence": "For the next article, I still thought three months was a reasonable timeframe. It took nine months from start to submission.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n20", "type": "milestone", "label": "Third article completed in five months from start to submission", "phase": 4, "evidence": "The third article took five months from start to submission.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n21", "type": "event", "label": "Became more efficient with time but still poor at estimating duration", "phase": 4, "evidence": "With practice and experience, I’ve certainly became more efficient with my time, but I’m still terrible at estimating how long something will take.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n22", "type": "event", "label": "Experienced feelings of stupidity and resentment due to delays and feedback", "phase": 4, "evidence": "For the longest time, the disconnection between my expectation of how long it should take and how long it was actually taking made me feel very stupid. They’ve all been doing relatively well. 1) PlayMyInbox got covered by MTV and Lifehacker, 2) Tubelytics was quickly adopted by some big media brands while 3) GoFuckingDoIt went completely viral and was featured all over the media including TheNextWeb, AppSumo and WIRED.

This month’s startup definitely went the best of them all though. And it might be the most successful thing I’ve built since I started my YouTube network Panda Mix Show years ago.

While traveling and working from different places in the world I met lots of other people doing the same thing.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Launch 12 MVP startups in 12 months to test hypotheses and find market fit", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I just launched my 4th startup called Nomad List as part of my goal to launch 12 startups in 12 months. They’re all minimum viable products, built to test a hypothesis and see if they can get a market fit in a month.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "goal", "label": "Create a city index / list for remote workers and digital nomads", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I knew some cities had entire communities doing this like Chiang Mai, but it was hard to figure out what other cities would be suitable.

As a software engineer, I’ve always loved the process of finding the product-market fit for an idea. {"source_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "A founder in Windsor, Canada, working at his first startup, becomes obsessed with a 'big idea' for a social news reader and ultimately builds a thriving telephony software business instead.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Working at first startup in Windsor with visa limits and moderate success turning to failure", "phase": 0, "evidence": "In the summer of 2003 while still working for my first startup... But I was in Windsor, Canada, far away from Silicon Valley and didn’t know anything about VCs or funding.
2003 was a tough year. My first startup was going from moderate success to disappointing failure very fast. I couldn’t do any consulting work because of my visa status.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Build a social news reader 'big idea'", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I’ve got a “big idea”: social news reader.
“It’s going to be huge!” – I thought.
So I was going to build everything myself.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Lack of RSS feeds, Facebook/social data, and users for the big idea", "phase": 1, "evidence": "In 2003 there was no Google Reader, no Facebook and hardly any RSS feeds. No RSS feeds? Ok, I will have to build an intelligent scraper that can crawl websites and gather news/updates. No Facebook to pull social data from? That’s a problem. I can’t build anything social without the people. I will need users to make it work, and a lot of them.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "action", "label": "Decides to build a simple free app to attract users", "phase": 1, "evidence": "My “big idea” was going to take a long time to build, so I decided to make something simple and give it away for free to attract users.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "action", "label": "Develops PhoneTray Free caller ID desktop app", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I had some experience with computer telephony, so small desktop app to show caller id was easy enough to develop. 2 months later PhoneTray Free was born.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Financial and motivational strain; close to giving up startups", "phase": 1, "evidence": "2003 was a tough year... Needless to say I wasn’t making tons of money 😉 I was very close to giving up on startups and accepting a full time job offer.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n7", "type": "action", "label": "Decides with wife to persist with own business", "phase": 1, "evidence": "But my wife had a job and we had some savings, so we decided to tough it up so I could continue with my own business.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n8", "type": "action", "label": "Works concurrently on big idea, first startup, and PhoneTray Free; users download the app", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I was working on my “big idea” and on what was left of my first startup, and people were downloading PhoneTray Free.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "event", "label": "Receives user email requesting call blocking feature", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I started getting emails from PhoneTray users, and they liked my little app. “Hey, I get annoying calls from my ex.” – one email said – “Can your program block calls from him?”.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "action", "label": "Implements blocking of calls from specific numbers in PhoneTray Free", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I thought “why not?” and implemented blocking of calls from specific numbers.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "milestone", "label": "PhoneTray Free becomes popular with hundreds of daily downloads", "phase": 2, "evidence": "And it was the feature that everyone wanted. PhoneTray Free was becoming popular. By the end of 2004 I was getting couple hundred downloads per day and tons of emails.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "event", "label": "Receives email from dial-up user about missing calls while online", "phase": 2, "evidence": "“I like your program and all” – one email said – “but what about us, dial-up internet users? We miss important calls when online!”.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "action", "label": "Researches dial-up usage and modem-on-hold situation", "phase": 2, "evidence": "“Um, really?” – I thought – “Is dial-up still alive?”. Quick Google search told me that over 65% of US internet users were still using dial-up at that time. But isn’t it a solved problem with modem-on-hold and V.92 standard? Apparently not, as I quickly found out.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n14", "type": "obstacle", "label": "No standard modem-on-hold API; undocumented, vendor-specific drivers", "phase": 2, "evidence": "V.92 standard describes how to implement call detection and modem-on-hold in hardware, but nothing about software or API. Windows doesn’t have built-in modem-on-hold support. There is a couple of modem-on-hold apps provided by modem manufacturers but they only work with specific modems, and most modems don’t come with any modem-on-hold software.
Well, turns out it’s not so easy. There is no standard way to implement modem-on-hold. Existing apps were talking directly to the modem driver using internal API. Undocumented of course. And each modem chipset vendor came up with its own API. Plus some vendors decided not to bother and didn’t implement any API.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n15", "type": "action", "label": "Studies modem drivers using assembler books and IDA; learns driver development", "phase": 3, "evidence": "So I got my old x86 assembler books and trusty IDA and started to look into how the modem drivers work. I disassembled several modem drivers, read up on driver development and figured out what I had to do.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "action", "label": "Designs and develops own kernel driver to control modem via PhoneTray", "phase": 3, "evidence": "I had to make my own kernel driver that sits on top of the modem driver and monitors what the modem driver is doing. Then PhoneTray can communicate with my driver and control the modem.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n17", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Complex, error-prone kernel driver development with debugging cycles", "phase": 3, "evidence": "Did I say that I like challenge?
