column2: Solo founder's report on Candy Japan crossing $10,000 MRR, from a Hacker News post to supermarket deals
column4: {"source_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "A Finnish founder living in Japan grows Candy Japan, a monthly surprise candy subscription, to over $10k MRR while streamlining sourcing, shipping, and support.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Running Candy Japan as a candy-of-the-month subscription", "phase": 0, "evidence": "Essentially Candy Japan is a \"candy of the month\" subscription service where I send subscribers random surprise candies twice each month in exchange for a monthly payment of $25.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Grow subscriber numbers and recurring revenue", "phase": 0, "evidence": "It grew thanks to several blog mentions to about 300 subscribers. For a long time it seemed the subscriber numbers wouldn't grow past that. But now I'm happy to report that ceiling has been shattered, and recurring monthly revenue has now crossed $10k", "certainty": "implied"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "action", "label": "Launch Candy Japan from a Hacker News post and comment thread", "phase": 1, "evidence": "It started from a simple HN post and a comment thread.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "milestone", "label": "Grow to about 300 subscribers via blog mentions", "phase": 1, "evidence": "It grew thanks to several blog mentions to about 300 subscribers.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Subscriber numbers appear stuck around 300", "phase": 1, "evidence": "For a long time it seemed the subscriber numbers wouldn't grow past that.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "outcome", "label": "Surpass past ceiling; cross $10k MRR with happy customers", "phase": 2, "evidence": "But now I'm happy to report that ceiling has been shattered, and recurring monthly revenue has now crossed $10k and customers are reporting that they are happy too.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n7", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Initial worry about customs issues", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Initially I worried about issues with customs", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n8", "type": "outcome", "label": "Packages generally arrive without customs trouble; minor single incident", "phase": 2, "evidence": "but based on surveys customers are reporting that they are receiving their packages without customs issues. Well, we did have one package where the customs officials opened it and checked whether a pouch of powder was actually candy or something more suspicious, but that is the only reported case out of thousands of packages sent and did not result in any trouble for us or the recipient.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Packages occasionally get returned due to address or delivery issues", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Sometimes packages do get returned to me (usually due to wrong address or customer not being home to accept a delivery)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "action", "label": "Resolve delivery issues with customers and resend packages", "phase": 2, "evidence": "but I always take the time to solve these issues with the customers and resend packages.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "outcome", "label": "Achieve profit comparable to a Japanese salaryman", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I've carved enough profit margin to reach an income level similar to a Japanese salaryman now.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "milestone", "label": "Spend enough on shipping that Japan Post staff know him by name", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I'm now spending enough on shipping that people at the post office know me by name.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "milestone", "label": "Ship 700 items in a single day", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Last time we sent 700 in a single day", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n14", "type": "milestone", "label": "Begin sending free review samples to bloggers and creators", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Lately a small part of those shipments is going for free to blog writers, YouTube video artists and other creative people who have showed an interest in possibly featuring Candy Japan. To help them write their posts or create their videos, I send some samples out.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n15", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Hesitated to offer free samples due to low measurable traffic", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Initially I hesitated to offer the free samples as it quite rarely results in any noticeable traffic at least in Google Analytics", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "action", "label": "Use extra candy pieces from full boxes as review samples", "phase": 2, "evidence": "but now I use these review samples to pad out the shipments. ... whenever I have a situation like that, I send those extra pieces to reviewers.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n17", "type": "outcome", "label": "Receive frequent review requests and some conversions", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I get email almost daily from blogs that want to review the shipments... Whether this is the best use for those extra pieces of candy I am not 100% sure, but it does result in some conversions.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n18", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Initially had to physically receive and ship boxes of candy from a third-floor apartment", "phase": 1, "evidence": "so there is no longer any need for me to physically receive boxes of candy. Which is great, since we live in the third floor with no elevator and it was getting a bit ridiculous to do all the shipping ourselves in the beginning", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n19", "type": "action", "label": "Establish and gradually build a sourcing and shipping relationship with a local supermarket", "phase": 1, "evidence": "Instead I chose the path of convenience, where I have an arrangement with a local supermarket. I give them suggestions on which candies I think foreigners might be interested in and they then contact the suppliers to see which ones they are able to get. ... Since this has been ongoing since 2011, I went from being a strange foreigner bothering the boss with requests for a few dozen extra packs of candy to being the \"Bemmu-kun\" who casually walks to the back room while employees are slurping noodles in their breaktime.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n20", "type": "outcome", "label": "Suppliers send items directly to supermarket; no need to receive boxes at home", "phase": 2, "evidence": "The suppliers send the items directly to the supermarket I am cooperating with, so there is no longer any need for me to physically receive boxes of candy.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n21", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Sacrifice margin for convenience by ordering via supermarket", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Having orders made for me is easy, but I am throwing away some margin there.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n22", "type": "milestone", "label": "Make first direct purchase from a manufacturer via HN-introduced contact", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I did make a small breakthrough recently by making the very first purchase directly from a manufacturer. It happened thanks to a fortunate connection I made through Hacker News. Through HN I got introduced to a coworking space in Osaka called Knowledge Salon (thanks @yuzool) and met someone there who is experienced in dealing with Japanese manufacturers. He helped make the initial phone call and thanks to his introduction we made the first order", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n23", "type": "milestone", "label": "Place first direct order for 550-piece variety box and gain manufacturer's trust", "phase": 2, "evidence": "we made the first order, which was for 550 pieces of a larger candy variety box, which was apparently a large enough order that they felt it was worth their time. After having the initial phone call made by a fluent Japanese person (and seeing money really getting transferred to their account), they were also willing to deal with me directly.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n24", "type": "outcome", "label": "Direct buying proves cheaper and allows larger shipment; learn phone/FAX preferred", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Obviously ordering from them was much cheaper than buying from the supermarket, which enabled me to send subscribers a larger shipment than usual that time. ... But it was encouraging to see that direct buying is possible. I also learned that phone and FAX were still preferred over email.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n25", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Manufacturer's selection limited to ramune candy", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Sadly that manufacturer only makes a certain type of candy (ramune) and their selection is too limited to make many orders from there in the future.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n26", "type": "action", "label": "Prepare shipping lists and have supermarket employees handle shipping", "phase": 2, "evidence": "after we decide what to send and the supermarket has received the items, I prepare a shipping list for them and the supermarket employees help do the shipping.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n27", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Originally wrote each customs form by hand", "phase": 1, "evidence": "We used to write each form by hand!", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n28", "type": "action", "label": "Develop Python script on Google App Engine to generate shipping PDFs with customs forms", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I have a Python script running in Google App Engine that gathers all the subscribers that are supposed to get a shipment and a PDF file is generated from those (complete with customs forms) that the supermarket can then print and attach to the packages.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n29", "type": "milestone", "label": "Establish ongoing, in-person collaboration with supermarket employees", "phase": 2, "evidence": "Our relationship still doesn't really feel much like \"drop shipping\", as I am physically meeting with the people there several times each month (and buying my groceries while there!). - Does it help our app get more users
- Does it help convert more users to paying customers
- Does it help users derive more value and ROI from the app
- Does it meaningfully improve user experience
- Does it reduce our support ticket load
- Does it have any unintended 2nd order consequences that can bite us later
Ultimately, you want to keep making decisions that move the needle for your business", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r2", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Design onboarding and product UX to minimize setup time and steps so users realize value as soon as possible", "evidence": "We wanted to enable our users to start using the app with the least amount of setup time or steps. This reflects in in the user experience of the app.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r3", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Provide sensible default configurations so first-time actions immediately trigger core functionality and value", "evidence": "We speed that up by automatically enabling the chat button on first save, along with the best default configuration for all chat button related settings.
Another example, when a user wants to start sending automated messages, all they have to do is click on the “Enable” button. All the app’s default configuration is automatically applied and the user can start seeing value immediately.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r4", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Offer fast, responsive customer support and proactive information beyond the immediate query", "evidence": "From day 1, we were clear on providing the best possible support. B- We proactively provide information beyond the immediate premise of the query", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r5", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Embed FAQs and answers to common questions directly within the product interface near relevant features", "evidence": "To solve this problem, we embedded FAQs inside the product itself.

2- does the feature align with the rest of our product
3- does the feature add core value to the user", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r10", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not build requested functionality that merely replaces other apps without enhancing your core product", "evidence": "Many times, we found users requesting features that would save them the hassle of using another app. Now, if that functionality enhances the rest of our app, it’s the right feature to add. Content marketing and Hacker News are essential to our growth even to this day.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r5", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Make the product fully open source to build trust, especially in privacy-first markets", "evidence": "Plausible goes fully open source with the MIT license, and all the code is made publicly available on GitHub.
We did this to be as transparent as possible and to give people more control over their data. Going open source is a great way to build trust in the privacy-first market that we operate in.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r6", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Split responsibilities between development and marketing so each can focus deeply", "evidence": "Running, developing and growing a startup in a competitive market such as web analytics is complicated. Uku could now focus entirely on the design and development of the product, while I could take care of the marketing, community management and customer support.
And with the two of us focused on different but equally essential tasks (development and marketing), we could make so much more progress than anyone can do on their own.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r7", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Define small, realistic growth goals (e.g., baseline organic traffic) and prioritize them", "evidence": "I’m a big fan of setting small but realistic goals, so my first tiny goal was to consistently get ten organic visitors from Google search per day.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r8", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Relauch and reposition the product to clearly communicate what it is and who it’s for", "evidence": "our first few weeks were spent on:
- Product relaunch (one example being that the early version of Plausible used one first-party cookie)
- New brand positioning (simple, lightweight, open source and privacy-first Google Analytics alternative)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r9", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Streamline naming and messaging for a consistent brand across all touchpoints", "evidence": "- Streamlining the communication to send a consistent message everywhere (as an example, previously, we used the name Plausible Insights in some places and Plausible Analytics in other places)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r10", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Improve site structure and consolidate content sections for clarity", "evidence": "- Improving the site structure (we used to have two different sections for content, one titled “journal” and the other “blog”, so we redirected the journal to the blog)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r11", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Create substantial product-related content, including positioning, comparisons, and feature-focused pages", "evidence": "- Adding a lot of new product-related content (each focus area of our positioning got one article, we published a comparison with Google Analytics and much more)", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r12", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Publish opinionated posts that clearly differentiate you from incumbents", "evidence": "Our new positioning was based on how different we are compared to Google Analytics, so we decided to pick a fight.
The post that changed our traction was: Why you should stop using Google Analytics on your website.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r13", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Proactively reach out to influential, relevant sites for coverage, accepting many will ignore you", "evidence": "This opportunity came as part of our outreach to different influential websites. Most sites ended up ignoring our messages. It isn’t easy to send so many emails and hear nothing back, but this one fabulous mention from a very relevant site was worth all that silence.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r14", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Invest in performance and scalable infrastructure to keep the product fast as you grow", "evidence": "With all the new trials and customers, and an increase in larger websites trying our service, Plausible became much slower to use. To continue our growth, we needed to improve the underlying technology that we use.
We moved from our PostgreSQL database to ClickHouse to make the app much faster and handle much bigger websites.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r15", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Treat major launch sites like Product Hunt as temporary boosts, not core growth channels", "evidence": "Product Hunt was worthwhile, but it’s not our core growth strategy, so it was just another day for us, albeit a bit busier. We didn’t put all of our eggs in this one basket.
Launching on community sites gives your project a spotlight for a day or two, but it’s not a sustainable channel to acquire customers in the long term. It brings that famous spike of hope after which follows the flat line of nope.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r16", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Adopt a sustainable funding model such as a premium managed cloud service while keeping code open", "evidence": "Running a premium managed service in the cloud while keeping the code open for inspection and self-hosting seems to be a better model for some open source projects such as our one.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r17", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Aim to make open source work financially without requiring personal financial sacrifice", "evidence": "Free and open source software can be sustainable and can pay your rent. Financial sacrifice is not required to work on open source.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r18", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Commit a fixed percentage of revenue to causes aligned with your values (e.g., environment, open source)", "evidence": "We decided to start giving back 5% of our gross revenue to environmental causes and open source.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r19", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Scale support by fixing, automating, and eliminating recurring issues rather than hiring a big support team", "evidence": "We think a lot about having a better user experience and being able to grow without needing to grow a customer support team too. We work hard on fixing, automating and eliminating issues that people encounter frequently. This reduces the number of customer support requests we’re getting.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r20", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Continuously invest in thorough, up-to-date documentation to reduce support load", "evidence": "We put a lot of effort into our docs, spend a lot of time on them and keep them up to date, answering any new questions we are getting. It has helped us scale our support to handle thousands of customers and trials without a dedicated support team.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r21", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Create timely content about industry news, adding your own perspective and unique value", "evidence": "If there are some news and happenings that you and your potential audience care about, create a post about it. Don’t just repeat the information everyone else is reporting but put your personal spin and point of view into it. Add something unique, informative and/or entertaining.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r22", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Use proprietary data and original studies to create compelling, differentiated content", "evidence": "Look at the opportunities in something only you have access to, such as in our case, the data we collect on website traffic. Do surveys, publish original studies. It’s a good way to get heard.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r23", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Hire only when the pain of not hiring becomes significant ("wait until it hurts")", "evidence": "What’s our strategy for hiring new people? How do we know when it’s time to hire? How do we define the skills needed? We follow the Basecamp approach. We wait until it hurts and only hire then.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r24", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Have everyone, including developers and founders, share responsibility for customer support", "evidence": "Everyone does some support at Plausible, and we don’t have any plans to hire dedicated support personnel with this approach.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r25", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Continuously maintain, bug-fix, and optimize infrastructure once product-market fit is reached", "evidence": "At some point, you find that product-market fit, that stable base where the roadmap becomes clear, and there’s much work to do to maintain it all. There’s a rhythm to things. We grow surely and steadily. But there’s a lot of hard work behind the scenes to make it all run smoothly.
We fix bugs. We engage with our community. We build new features. We respond to people reaching out to us. We work on our infrastructure to handle the increased demand. We think long-term, optimize what needs to be optimized and carefully organize things to stay stable.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r26", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Position the product to benefit from regulatory and market shifts and then act quickly to seize them", "evidence": "Plausible was well positioned in this market, so immediately after this announcement, we saw an increase in interest in our product and service.
We’ve tried our best to seize the opportunities that presented themselves to us. We worked hard to be the well-positioned alternative to Google Analytics both from the privacy and Universal Analytics/GA4 perspectives.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r27", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Build migration tools that ease switching from incumbents (e.g., imports, missing features)", "evidence": "We introduced an import tool that allows people to bring their old Google Analytics stats into Plausible.
We also have a realtime dashboard and a landing page report which many Google Analytics users are unhappy about with their Google Analytics experience. This has helped make Plausible an excellent alternative to an increasing number of sites unhappy with Google’s approach.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r28", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Focus on building a great product people enjoy and want to recommend as the core growth driver", "evidence": "We focus on a small number of things, but we try to do them as best as we can:
- Build a great product that people enjoy using and want to recommend. This is the key, as nothing else would work without a great product.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r29", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Publish mission-driven content that clearly states your beliefs and stance", "evidence": "- We publish content on our blog and social media, communicating what we believe in and stand for. We take a stand and hope it resonates with as many people as possible.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r30", "primitive": "Repeat", "label": "Continue doing what works and give growth time, focusing on calm, organic progress", "evidence": "We will continue to focus on things that have worked well for us and see how it goes.
The best answer I have for how and when we will reach $1M ARR is simply giving it time and being patient. We will get there naturally and organically by taking it one day at a time and de-Googling one website at a time.", "certainty": "stated", "stop_condition": "reaching desired sustainable ARR milestones (e.g., $1M ARR) or until conditions change materially"}, {"id": "r31", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Run the company calmly without pursuit of hyper-growth or world domination targets", "evidence": "We’re trying to run a calm company without world-dominating growth targets and with the focus on having a great product that helps people solve the issues they have with Google Analytics.
We’re not interested in venture capitalism, in the chase for the endless hyper-growth, or in building a unicorn. We don’t have any goals about world domination.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r32", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not use paid advertising as part of the marketing strategy", "evidence": "We don’t use paid advertising", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r33", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not use spy pixels, retargeting, session recordings, popups, or intrusive calls to action", "evidence": "We don’t use spy pixels and retargeting
We don’t use session recordings
We don’t do popups and other intrusive calls to action", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r34", "primitive": "NOT", "label": "Do not pay for promotion, chatbots for conversion, or link buying for SEO", "evidence": "We don’t pay anyone to promote or recommend us
We don’t use a chat bot to engage you or convert you
We don’t participate in any link buying for SEO purposes", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r35", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Make cancellation easy and notify users before renewals to avoid surprises", "evidence": "In addition to this, we make it very easy to cancel a subscription at any time. No need to contact us. No questions are asked.
We also inform people a few days before their annual subscription is up for renewal to give them a chance to cancel in case they no longer find Plausible useful. There are no surprise fees, and we never charge anyone unexpectedly either.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r36", "primitive": "Op", "label": "Aim to build a sustainable business aligned with a clear mission rather than maximizing valuation", "evidence": "We aim to continue building a sustainable business that helps us remain true to our mission of removing Google Analytics from as many websites as possible and bringing privacy-first, open source software to more people.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "r37", "primitive": "AND", "label": "Combine product quality, content marketing, transparency, and ethical practices as the growth engine", "evidence": "Our marketing strategy has been remarkably similar throughout all the different milestones. It’s not based on shouting, interrupting or tricking people. It’s a boring strategy and doesn’t feature any exciting growth hacks.
We focus on a small number of things, but we try to do them as best as we can:
- Build a great product that people enjoy using and want to recommend.
- We publish content on our blog and social media, communicating what we believe in and stand for.

{"source_id": "unknown", "subject_summary": "Rob Picard, a security engineer who left his role at Robinhood in 2020 to start Observa, an intrusion detection/security tooling company, which he later shut down and then joined Vanta and became active in venture investing.", "nodes": [{"id": "n1", "type": "start_state", "label": "Security professional at companies like Addepar and Robinhood, long-time Hacker News reader wanting to start a software company", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I’ve been in the security industry for a little over eight years. I started off as a penetration tester at Matasano Security and eventually worked on application security, intrusion detection, and incident response at companies like Addepar and Robinhood.

I’ve been reading Hacker News since I was 14, and I always knew I’d eventually want to start a software company.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n2", "type": "goal", "label": "Start a software/security company and become a successful entrepreneur", "phase": 0, "evidence": "I always knew I’d eventually want to start a software company.

I wanted to be a successful entrepreneur, but I didn’t want to spend years searching for the right idea.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n3", "type": "milestone", "label": "Read The Launchpad and decided to apply to Y Combinator with a security idea", "phase": 1, "evidence": "In late 2020, I read The Launchpad for the first time, and I decided to apply to Y Combinator with an idea I had been considering.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n4", "type": "milestone", "label": "Accepted to Y Combinator and left Robinhood to start building Observa", "phase": 1, "evidence": "I decided to apply to Y Combinator with an idea I had been considering. I was accepted, and I left Robinhood to start building.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n5", "type": "action", "label": "Started Observa to build a lightweight intrusion detection system for early-stage companies", "phase": 2, "evidence": "The original idea for Observa was to build a lightweight intrusion detection system targeting earlier-stage companies.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n6", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Faced obstacles: important log sources hard to access, required enterprise tiers, and had delayed data", "phase": 2, "evidence": "I quickly realized that there were a few obstacles to building something like this that would provide value to smaller startups. Some of the most important log sources that I wanted to monitor were difficult to access or required enterprise-tier subscriptions to the products. My idea was to work with these service providers and have them share the IP addresses that were performing these attacks in real time.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n9", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Could not get major consumer companies to pilot or share IPs; many lacked real-time detection and blocking tooling", "phase": 3, "evidence": "Long story short, everyone thought this was cool, but after months of trying, I couldn’t get any of these major consumer companies to try a pilot and share some of the IPs they detected. It also turned out that many of them didn’t have sophisticated enough detection capabilities to produce a list of IP addresses in real-time, nor did they have the tooling to block new IPs that I might provide in real-time.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n10", "type": "action", "label": "Pivoted again to focus Observa on detecting public database exposure in AWS accounts", "phase": 4, "evidence": "I changed direction again and decided to “do one thing well” with a product that would detect public database exposure in AWS accounts.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n11", "type": "action", "label": "Built the AWS public database exposure detection tool and launched it on Product Hunt", "phase": 4, "evidence": "I built this tool, launched it on Product Hunt, and a handful of people signed up to use it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n12", "type": "milestone", "label": "Acquired a handful of initial users after Product Hunt launch", "phase": 4, "evidence": "launched it on Product Hunt, and a handful of people signed up to use it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n13", "type": "action", "label": "Tried paid ads to grow Observa but found no real traction", "phase": 5, "evidence": "I tried paid ads but didn’t find any real traction.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n14", "type": "action", "label": "Offered YC startups a shared Slack channel for security advice and engaged with their questions", "phase": 5, "evidence": "I did later put out an offer to all YC startups that I would join their Slack workspace with a shared channel and provide security advice, etc. I got a great response from that, but most of the questions ended up being about issues blocking sales (compliance, questionnaires) as opposed to security issues.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n15", "type": "obstacle", "label": "Final iteration users uninterested in findings; product not solving a burning issue they’d pay for", "phase": 6, "evidence": "With the final iteration of Observa, I found that startups who were interested enough to sign up for a free trial and hook up the tool to their AWS account weren’t really interested in the findings that came out of it. It wasn’t solving a burning issue for them, and they weren’t going to pay for it.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n16", "type": "event", "label": "Realized after a year of changing direction that he didn’t want to keep going with Observa", "phase": 7, "evidence": "After a year of changing direction without any good ideas for the next thing, I just realized that I didn’t want to do it anymore.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n17", "type": "event", "label": "Decided to stop taking payment from Observa and spend indefinite time figuring out the next idea", "phase": 7, "evidence": "I emailed my investors to tell them I was going to stop taking any payment from the company and spend an indefinite amount of time figuring out the next idea.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n18", "type": "event", "label": "Decided after a month or two to return remaining money and shut Observa down", "phase": 7, "evidence": "After a month or two, I let them know I was going to return the rest of the money and shut down.", "certainty": "stated"}, {"id": "n19", "type": "outcome", "label": "Shut down Observa after working on it for 10 months, returning most of the raised capital and generating no revenue", "phase": 8, "evidence": "I worked on Observa for 10 months, from November 2020 to September 2021.
